pharm: An H2-receptor antagonist that reduces gastric acid secretion, used for peptic ulcer disease and reflux; marketed outside the USA, not FDA-approved

Can be taken with or without food; night dose common
Use only if clearly needed; limited data
Caution; H2 antagonists are excreted in milk
Reduce dose in renal impairment (renally eliminated)
Usually no major adjustment; use cautiously in severe impairment
No specific interaction; alcohol may aggravate ulcer disease
Symptom response; renal function for dosing; exclude gastric malignancy
summary: Roxatidine (administered as the prodrug roxatidine acetate) is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist that reduces basal and stimulated gastric acid secretion. It is used to treat and prevent peptic (gastric and duodenal) ulcers, reflux oesophagitis and other acid-related disorders, and for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. The active metabolite is roxatidine; a typical regimen is 150 mg once daily at bedtime or 75 mg twice daily for active disease, with 75 mg at night for maintenance. It is marketed in Europe, Japan and parts of Asia (e.g. as Roxit/Roxan) and is NOT FDA-approved, so this monograph is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF-type sources. It is largely renally eliminated, so the dose should be reduced in renal impairment. It is generally well tolerated; unlike cimetidine it has minimal antiandrogenic and CYP-enzyme-inhibition effects, so fewer drug interactions are expected. As with all acid suppressants, response to therapy should not mask an underlying gastric malignancy.
indications: Treatment of benign gastric and duodenal ulcer
Reflux oesophagitis and symptomatic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and other hypersecretory conditions
Prevention of stress ulceration/acid aspiration where indicated

dosage.d: 150 mg once daily at bedtime, OR 75 mg twice daily
dosage.t: Oral; night dose taken before bed
dosage.n: Course usually 4-8 weeks depending on indication

dosage.d: Reduce dose/frequency (e.g. 75 mg once daily) when creatinine clearance is significantly reduced

admin: Take orally; the once-daily dose is usually given at bedtime
May be taken with or without food
Reduce the dose in significant renal impairment, as roxatidine is mainly excreted by the kidneys
Exclude gastric malignancy before treating gastric ulcer, as symptom relief can mask cancer
Use the shortest effective course for the indication
moa: Roxatidine acetate is a prodrug hydrolysed by esterases to the active compound roxatidine, a competitive antagonist at histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells. By blocking histamine-mediated stimulation it reduces basal, nocturnal and stimulated (food-, gastrin- and pentagastrin-induced) gastric acid secretion and lowers gastric acid output, promoting healing of acid-related mucosal disease. It has little affinity for androgen receptors and minimal inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, giving it a more favourable interaction profile than cimetidine.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to roxatidine or to other H2-receptor antagonists
relative: Pregnancy and breastfeeding (use only if clearly needed)
Suspected gastric malignancy not yet excluded
monitor: Exclusion of underlying malignancy in gastric ulcer

preg: There are limited data on roxatidine in pregnancy. It should be used during pregnancy only if clearly necessary and the expected benefit outweighs any potential risk.
lact: H2-receptor antagonists are excreted in breast milk. Caution is advised; use only if the benefit justifies the potential risk to the infant, or consider withholding breastfeeding.
renal: Roxatidine is eliminated predominantly by the kidneys, so the dose should be reduced (for example to 75 mg once daily) in patients with significant renal impairment, with adjustment guided by creatinine clearance.
hepatic: No major dose adjustment is generally needed for hepatic impairment; use with caution in severe liver disease and monitor clinically.

moderate: Drugs requiring an acidic gastric environment for absorption (e.g. ketoconazole, itraconazole, atazanavir) - reduced absorption due to higher gastric pH
minor: Antacids may reduce roxatidine absorption if taken at the same time - separate dosing
interactions.food: Can be taken with or without food; no major food interaction
interactions.alcohol: No specific pharmacologic interaction; alcohol may aggravate acid-peptic disease
interactions.diagnostics: Acid suppression can affect gastric pH-dependent tests; may need to be withheld before some diagnostic gastric acid or urea breath testing

serious: Blood dyscrasias (rare for the H2-antagonist class)
rare: Confusion in the elderly or in renal impairment (less than with cimetidine)
Gynaecomastia (much less likely than with cimetidine)

monitoring: Renal function to guide dosing in impairment
Exclusion of gastric malignancy in patients treated for gastric ulcer
Liver enzymes and blood counts if clinically indicated
counsel: This medicine reduces stomach acid to heal and prevent ulcers and reflux
Take it as prescribed, often at night, and complete the full course even once symptoms improve
Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems, as the dose may need to be lower
Report persistent stomach pain, difficulty swallowing, weight loss, vomiting or black stools, which need investigation
Avoid taking antacids at the same time; separate them by a couple of hours
pk: Acid suppression within about 1 hour of dosing
Active roxatidine plasma peak roughly 3 hours after oral roxatidine acetate
Elimination half-life of active roxatidine approximately 4-6 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Acid suppression lasts up to about 12 hours, supporting once- or twice-daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from moisture, per product label
pearls: NOTE: Roxatidine is NOT FDA-approved; it is marketed in Europe, Japan and parts of Asia - this monograph is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF-type sources
It is the acetate prodrug, hydrolysed to active roxatidine, with night-time once-daily dosing an option (150 mg nocte or 75 mg BID)
Mainly renally eliminated - reduce the dose in renal impairment
Compared with cimetidine it has minimal CYP inhibition and antiandrogen effect, so fewer interactions and less gynaecomastia
Exclude gastric malignancy before treating a gastric ulcer, as acid suppression can mask cancer
Separate from antacids and watch reduced absorption of pH-dependent drugs (azole antifungals, atazanavir)
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose experience is limited; expected effects are extensions of pharmacology (e.g. drowsiness). There is no specific antidote. Manage supportively with symptomatic treatment and monitoring; haemodialysis may remove some drug given its renal elimination, but is rarely required.
